claims.text: The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type alloy is non-equiatomic.
Physical vapor deposition produces an ordered, single-phase hexagonal structure in the as-deposited films.
Low-temperature post-deposition annealing improves short-range atomic ordering at grain boundaries.
Improved short-range ordering reduces internal strain.
Reduced internal strain facilitates a more gradual magnetostructural transition.
A more gradual magnetostructural transition lowers hysteresis without significantly reducing the magnetocaloric entropy-change magnitude.
Annealing at 300–400°C can optimize local chemical order while limiting grain growth and phase segregation.
Annealing enhances short-range chemical ordering both at grain boundaries and within the bulk of the film.
Enhanced chemical ordering reduces internal stress and crystalline-lattice strain.
Defect reduction and stress relief improve coupling between the magnetic and lattice subsystems.
Improved magnetic–lattice coupling smooths the magnetostructural transition.
Annealed films will exhibit a modestly broader transition-temperature range than as-deposited films.
Annealed films will exhibit significantly reduced hysteresis width relative to the as-deposited baseline.
Annealed films will retain a magnetocaloric entropy-change magnitude comparable to the as-deposited baseline.
As-deposited films undergo a sharp, first-order magnetostructural transition producing a large but hysteretic entropy change.
The as-deposited films have limited heat-exchange performance because of a low surface-to-volume ratio.
The prediction applies only when annealing remains below a phase-instability or phase-segregation threshold.
Annealing above the critical threshold may cause adverse effects.

contradictions.description: The material is consistently described as a thin film, but the baseline attributes poor heat exchange to a low surface-to-volume ratio. That limitation belongs to bulk ingots or ribbons in the task context and is inconsistent with the thin-film geometry proposed to enable rapid heat exchange.
